Third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board for garment workers held; sporadic protests and clashes continue today in the Gazipur-Ashulia industrial belt; over a hundred factories have declared a shutdown.
Police state that Constable Anwar was murdered by drug traffickers in Fatullah, Narayanganj; law enforcement agencies have yet to apprehend anyone involved.

snippet.title: O BÁSICO que NINGUÉM FAZ (10 hábitos para colocar sua vida em ordem)
snippet.description:
🔥 8 coisas que PAREI DE FAZER depois de entender NEUROCIÊNCIA ▶ https://youtu.be/urLAA30gFXM

🔥 É ISSO que o CELULAR faz com SEU CÉREBRO (neurociência) ▶https://youtu.be/ov7iicMiPNQ


_________________________

Como organizar a vida, ter disciplina e parar de procrastinar? Neste vídeo do canal NeuroVox, o professor e neurocientista Pedro Calabrez apresenta 10 hábitos simples para colocar a vida em ordem, organizar a rotina e sair do piloto automático.

O vídeo começa com a história de Ivan McGuire, um paraquedista experiente que saltou sem o paraquedas. A partir desse caso, Pedro mostra como é fácil deixar o básico passar despercebido e leva essa reflexão à rotina de quem passa o dia apagando incêndios.

Pedro conta que costumava dizer que odiava rotina e explica o que mudou quando passou a planejar o dia na véspera e a retomar o plano depois dos imprevistos. Com exemplos do dia a dia e ideias da psicologia e da neurociência, o vídeo aborda como organizar melhor o tempo, criar hábitos que duram e reservar espaço para a saúde e para as pessoas importantes. Também trata da reciprocidade nos relacionamentos e de como distinguir emoções e fatos na hora de tomar decisões difíceis.

🔎 PERGUNTAS QUE O VÍDEO RESPONDE

• Como organizar melhor o tempo? 

• Como ter disciplina e constância? 

• O que fazer para parar de procrastinar? 

• O que fazer para ter foco e concentração? 

• Como dormir melhor e acordar mais disposto? 

Qual desses hábitos faria mais diferença na rotina? A conversa continua nos comentários. Para acompanhar novos vídeos do professor #PedroCalabrez sobre #autoconhecimento e desenvolvimento pessoal com ciência, basta se inscrever no canal #NeuroVox .

snippet.title: How did monks grow barley on a treeless rock, 12 km out in the Atlantic?
snippet.description:
What happened: a spike of rock rises from the Atlantic, about 12 kilometers off the coast of Ireland. Near the top, stone huts cling to the ledges. No trees grow here, and almost no soil covers the rock. Yet monks lived up there for centuries. The rock is Skellig Michael, and its highest peak stands 218 meters above the water. More than 1,200 years ago, Vikings attacked, yet the community stayed. So how did monks grow food up there?

The problem: every farm needs flat ground, soil and water. The rock had almost none. The slopes are steep, salt spray blows across them, and rainwater pours right off the bare stone. There is not one tree, so firewood came by boat, and from October to May boats often cannot land.

How it worked: the answer begins at the water, where about 600 stone steps climb from the sea. Monks built tall stone walls across the slope, and behind each wall the gap became flat ground: level terraces, like giant steps. For soil, monks carried up seaweed from the shore. Seaweed went into the soil, and human manure went in too. Think of a garden box on a balcony: the box holds the earth, and scraps keep the earth rich. On these terraces, monks grew barley and oats, and grinding stones made flour from the grain. Water came from the sky: rock-cut channels guide rainwater into stone tanks. The sea gave fish, and the cliffs gave seabirds. Boats from the mainland probably brought extra grain and firewood.

How we know: archaeologists dug there. Tiny insect remains in the garden soil point to seaweed and manure, and burnt puffin bones turned up too.

The part almost nobody knows: higher still, just below the South Peak, hermits built tiny terraces. One terrace was a garden about 13 meters long. Basins cut into the rock caught rain, and earth for that garden came up from below. In places, the ledge hangs over a 70-meter drop. In 1986, a survey team worked up there on ropes.

Visuals: AI-assisted 3D visualization; the monastery scenes, the hermitage and the dig are schematic reconstructions. The island today has a lighthouse road and visitor railings, left out here. Dates and figures: real and rounded. Sources:
- UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sceilg Mhichil (No. 757)
- Office of Public Works, Sceilg Mhichil World Heritage Property: Site and Safety Guide
- J. Crowley and J. Sheehan (eds), The Book of the Skelligs (Cork University Press, 2022), summarized in Current Archaeology 398 (2023)
- W. Horn, J. White Marshall and G. D. Rourke, The Forgotten Hermitage of Skellig Michael (University of California Press, 1990)
- Annals of Ulster, entry for 824 (Etgal of Scelec)
- E. Bourke, Skellig Michael Monks' Garden excavation summaries, excavations.ie (1994, 1995)
